stem: Which long-term factor contributed to tensions before the First World War?

options.text: Rivalry among European powers over empire and influence
The creation of the United Nations
The dissolution of the Ottoman Empire after 1945

explanation: Imperial rivalry contributed to tensions, alongside militarism, alliance systems and nationalism; historians do not treat one factor as the sole cause.

stem: Which countries formed the Triple Entente before the First World War?

options.text: Britain, Germany and the Ottoman Empire

explanation: The Triple Entente linked Britain, France and Russia before the war.

stem: Which states were members of the Triple Alliance before the war began?
explanation: The prewar Triple Alliance comprised Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy; Italy later joined the Allies in 1915.

stem: Why did the alliance system contribute to the widening of the 1914 crisis?

options.text: It required every country to remain neutral
It prevented mobilisation by member states
It replaced national armies with one European force
It could draw additional powers into a conflict between Austria-Hungary and Serbia

explanation: Alliance commitments and strategic calculations helped widen the conflict, though they did not make war automatic.

stem: Which statement about militarism before 1914 is accurate?

options.text: Military planning and arms competition formed part of the broader climate of tension
It meant European states had abolished their armies
It was a policy adopted only after the 1918 armistice
It required Britain and Germany to share one navy

explanation: Military planning and an arms race contributed to tension, particularly among the great powers.

stem: Which statement best explains the role of nationalism before 1914?

options.text: Nationalism had disappeared from European politics
Nationalist demands and rivalries affected several regions and could intensify international tensions
It applied only to overseas colonies
It made the alliance system irrelevant

explanation: Nationalism affected both great-power rivalry and movements within multiethnic empires; it interacted with other causes.

stem: Which pair names two long-term causes often used to explain the outbreak of the First World War?

options.text: The Treaty of Rome and the Cold War

explanation: Alliance rivalry and militarism are two of the long-term factors commonly discussed alongside imperialism and nationalism.

stem: Which conclusion about the causes of the First World War is best supported?

options.text: The assassination alone explains every cause of the war
A treaty signed in 1919 caused the war in 1914
The war began because all European states belonged to one alliance
Several long-term tensions interacted with the July Crisis; no single cause alone explains the outbreak

explanation: The war grew from interacting long-term tensions and a specific diplomatic crisis; reducing it to one cause oversimplifies the evidence.

stem: Who was assassinated at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914?
explanation: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was assassinated in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914.

stem: Which organisation did Gavrilo Princip belong to?
explanation: Princip was associated with Young Bosnia, a revolutionary nationalist movement in Bosnia.

stem: When did Austria-Hungary declare war on Serbia in 1914?
explanation: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914, one month after the assassination.

stem: What did Austria-Hungary send to Serbia on 23 July 1914?
explanation: Austria-Hungary delivered an ultimatum to Serbia on 23 July; the response and subsequent decisions formed part of the July Crisis.

stem: Which state did Germany declare war on first in August 1914?
explanation: Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August 1914, followed by declarations on France and Belgium’s invasion.

stem: Why did Britain enter the war against Germany in August 1914?

options.text: Germany’s invasion of Belgium was a central immediate factor in Britain’s declaration
Britain had signed the Treaty of Versailles
The United States requested it to join

explanation: Germany invaded Belgium on 4 August; Britain declared war later that day, with strategic and treaty considerations involved.

stem: Which sequence correctly orders the opening of the July Crisis?

options.text: Assassination at Sarajevo → Austro-Hungarian ultimatum to Serbia → Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia

explanation: The assassination occurred on 28 June, the ultimatum was delivered on 23 July, and Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July 1914.

stem: What turned the conflict between Austria-Hungary and Serbia into a wider European war?

options.text: A unanimous vote of the League of Nations
The signing of the Treaty of Versailles
The withdrawal of all great powers from Europe
Mobilisation, declarations of war and alliance decisions involving other powers

explanation: Mobilisation and a chain of diplomatic and military decisions widened the crisis; the process was not simply an automatic treaty mechanism.

stem: On which front was the trench warfare of the Western Front concentrated?

options.text: Along the Pacific coast of China
In the Alps between Italy and Switzerland only

explanation: The Western Front ran principally through Belgium and northern France and became associated with entrenched warfare.

stem: Which battle on the Western Front began in February 1916?
explanation: The Battle of Verdun began in February 1916 and continued until December.

stem: When did the Battle of the Somme begin?
explanation: The Somme offensive began on 1 July 1916 on the Western Front.

stem: What was the main strategic aim of the Allied Gallipoli campaign?

options.text: Reach the Russian capital by land from France
Protect the Suez Canal from an Italian invasion
Open a sea route through the Dardanelles and pressure the Ottoman Empire

explanation: The campaign aimed to force the Dardanelles, threaten Constantinople and open a supply route to Russia.

stem: Which battle took place on the Eastern Front in 1914 and became an early German victory over Russia?
explanation: German forces defeated Russian armies at Tannenberg in August 1914.

stem: Which naval battle in 1916 was fought between the British and German fleets?
explanation: The Battle of Jutland took place in the North Sea in 1916 between the main British and German fleets.

stem: What characterised much of the Western Front between 1914 and 1918?

options.text: A continuous mobile advance across the entire front
A ceasefire that lasted from 1914 to 1918
Trench lines and repeated offensives with heavy losses

explanation: Long trench systems and repeated offensives marked much of the Western Front, though tactics and front conditions changed over time.

stem: Which sequence correctly orders the opening of three major battles?
explanation: The Gallipoli campaign began in 1915, followed by Verdun in February 1916 and the Somme in July 1916.

stem: Which automatic weapon made exposed infantry especially vulnerable during trench warfare?
explanation: Machine guns, artillery and barbed wire made attacks across exposed ground especially dangerous.

stem: What was the purpose of unrestricted submarine warfare announced by Germany in 1917?

options.text: To protect all neutral merchant ships
To attack shipping without the earlier restrictions on warning or targeting
To end the naval blockade of Germany
To transfer the German fleet to the United States

explanation: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare in 1917, increasing risks to neutral and Allied shipping.

stem: When were tanks first used by British forces in battle during the war?
explanation: British tanks were first used in battle during the Somme campaign in September 1916.

stem: Which comparison between Verdun and the Somme is accurate?

options.text: Both were fought against the Ottoman Empire at sea
Verdun took place after the 1918 armistice
The Somme preceded the assassination at Sarajevo
Both were major Western Front battles in 1916, but they began at different times and had distinct operational aims

explanation: Verdun began in February 1916; the Somme began in July. Both became major and costly Western Front battles.

stem: Which empire joined the Central Powers during the First World War?
explanation: The Ottoman Empire entered the war on the side of the Central Powers in 1914.

stem: When did the United States declare war on Germany?
explanation: The United States declared war on Germany in April 1917.

stem: Which development was one factor in the United States’ 1917 decision to enter the war?

options.text: The signing of the Treaty of Versailles
The outbreak of the Russian Civil War in 1918
Germany’s resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare
The creation of the League of Nations

explanation: Unrestricted submarine warfare was a major factor; the Zimmermann Telegram and other considerations also shaped U.S. policy.

stem: What did wartime mobilisation mean for many civilian economies?

options.text: All factories closed for the duration
Women were excluded from every wartime job
Governments redirected labour and production toward the war effort

explanation: Wartime governments mobilised industry, labour and resources on a large scale; experiences differed by country.

stem: Which statement about colonial troops in the First World War is accurate?

options.text: Soldiers and labourers from European empires served in multiple theatres
They served only after the war ended
They fought exclusively on the Western Front
No colonial subjects took part in the war

explanation: People from imperial territories served as soldiers and labourers across several fronts and theatres.

stem: Which region was part of the Middle Eastern theatre of the war?
explanation: The Mesopotamian campaign was one of the war’s Middle Eastern theatres.

stem: Which statement best captures the global character of the First World War?

options.text: It was fought only between France and Germany
It involved no naval or overseas campaigns
It involved empires, colonies, overseas theatres and economic mobilisation beyond Europe
It ended before the Ottoman Empire joined

explanation: The conflict extended beyond Europe through imperial forces, overseas campaigns, naval operations and global economic mobilisation.

stem: Which pair correctly matches a development with its year?
explanation: The United States entered the war in 1917; the armistice followed in 1918 and the Treaty of Versailles in 1919.

stem: On what date did the armistice ending the fighting on the Western Front take effect?
explanation: The armistice took effect on 11 November 1918.

stem: Which event led Russia to leave the First World War?

options.text: The February Revolution restored Nicholas II
The Bolshevik government signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
The Treaty of Versailles was signed
The United States entered the war

explanation: The Bolshevik government negotiated a separate peace with Germany at Brest-Litovsk in March 1918.

stem: What was the date of the Treaty of Versailles with Germany?
explanation: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919, months after the armistice ended the fighting.

stem: Which statement distinguishes an armistice from a peace treaty?

options.text: An armistice creates a new empire; a peace treaty declares war
Both terms mean the same thing
A peace treaty must be signed before fighting begins
An armistice stops fighting; a peace treaty sets formal postwar terms

explanation: The 11 November 1918 armistice ended active fighting; the 1919 peace treaties established formal settlements.

stem: Which event took place in 1917 and helped alter the military balance of the war?

options.text: The United States entered the war while Russia underwent revolution
The Treaty of Versailles was signed

explanation: The United States entered the war in 1917, while revolution in Russia led to a later withdrawal from the conflict.

stem: When did the German Spring Offensive begin?
explanation: Germany began its major Spring Offensive in March 1918 after Russia’s withdrawal enabled the transfer of forces west.

stem: Which sequence correctly orders the end of the war and the peace settlement with Germany?
explanation: Russia’s separate peace came in March 1918, the armistice in November 1918, and the Versailles treaty in June 1919.

stem: Why should the armistice and the Treaty of Versailles not be treated as the same event?

options.text: The Treaty ended the war before the armistice began
The armistice applied only to Russia and Versailles only to Italy
They occurred on different dates and served different purposes: one stopped fighting, the other set peace terms

explanation: The armistice stopped fighting in November 1918; the Versailles treaty established terms with Germany in June 1919.

stem: Which Russian ruler abdicated during the February Revolution of 1917?
explanation: Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917 by the Gregorian calendar, during the revolution known in Russia as the February Revolution under the Julian calendar.

stem: Which government replaced the tsarist monarchy after the February Revolution?
explanation: The Provisional Government assumed authority after Nicholas II’s abdication, alongside the growing influence of the soviets.

stem: Why is the February Revolution also dated to March 1917 in many accounts?

options.text: The event occurred in two different Russian capitals
Russia then used the Julian calendar, which was 13 days behind the Gregorian calendar
All European countries used the Julian calendar

explanation: The February Revolution’s dates are often given in both styles: February in the Julian calendar and March in the Gregorian calendar.

stem: What political arrangement is often called “dual power” in Russia in 1917?

options.text: The tsar and the German emperor ruled jointly
Two monarchs governed Moscow and Petrograd
The League of Nations shared authority with the Bolsheviks
The Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet both claimed political authority

explanation: The Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet were competing centres of authority after the February Revolution.

stem: Which group seized power in Petrograd during the October Revolution?
explanation: Bolshevik forces overthrew the Provisional Government in Petrograd in November 1917 by the Gregorian calendar.

stem: Which sequence correctly orders the Russian Revolutions and Russia’s exit from the war?

options.text: Brest-Litovsk → February Revolution → Bolshevik seizure of power
February Revolution → Bolshevik seizure of power → Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
Bolshevik seizure of power → Treaty of Brest-Litovsk → February Revolution
February Revolution → Brest-Litovsk → Bolshevik seizure of power

explanation: The February Revolution came first in 1917, the Bolsheviks seized power later that year, and the treaty was signed in March 1918.

stem: Which slogan summarised Bolshevik demands in 1917?
explanation: Bolshevik slogans addressed demands for peace, land and relief from shortages; wording and emphasis varied across campaigns.

stem: Which decree did the Bolsheviks issue soon after taking power in 1917?
explanation: The new Bolshevik government issued a Decree on Peace calling for an end to the war and negotiations.

stem: What did the Bolshevik Decree on Land address?

options.text: The transfer of land from large estates to peasant control
The division of the Ottoman Empire

explanation: The Decree on Land endorsed redistribution and the seizure of landed estates, reflecting peasant demands.

stem: What was the main consequence of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk for Russia?

options.text: It brought Russia into the war against Germany
It ended Russia’s participation in the First World War at a high territorial cost
It established the League of Nations

explanation: The treaty ended Russia’s war with the Central Powers but required substantial territorial concessions.

stem: Which power signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Soviet Russia in March 1918?
explanation: Germany signed the treaty with Soviet Russia on 3 March 1918.

stem: Which event followed Russia’s withdrawal from the First World War?

options.text: The armistice immediately ended fighting on every front
The United States left the war
The Treaty of Versailles was signed the next day
Germany could transfer forces from the Eastern Front, although the war continued elsewhere

explanation: Russia’s exit freed German forces for the Western Front, but fighting continued until the November 1918 armistice.

stem: Which sequence correctly places the assassination, the United States’ entry and the armistice?
explanation: The assassination triggered the July Crisis in 1914; the United States entered in 1917; the armistice took effect in 1918.

stem: Which statement best connects the Russian Revolutions to the First World War?

options.text: The revolutions immediately ended the war for all combatants
The revolutions changed Russia’s government and ultimately led the Bolsheviks to withdraw from the war
The February Revolution brought the United States into the war
The revolutions created the Treaty of Versailles in 1917

explanation: The 1917 revolutions transformed Russian politics; the Bolshevik government later signed a separate peace in 1918.

stem: Which statement best summarises the war’s ending?

options.text: The Treaty of Versailles ended fighting in 1914
The Russian treaty of 1918 ended every front in Europe
An armistice stopped the fighting in 1918, while peace treaties followed in 1919 and after
The war ended when the United States entered in 1917

explanation: The armistice stopped active fighting in November 1918; formal peace settlements followed, beginning with Versailles in 1919.

stem: Which summary best describes the First World War’s causes and course?

options.text: One alliance automatically caused war and ended it in 1916
The conflict was confined to one trench line in France
The Russian Revolution preceded all prewar tensions
Long-term rivalries interacted with a diplomatic crisis, and warfare spread across fronts and empires before separate armistice and peace-settlement stages

explanation: Multiple tensions and diplomatic decisions led to a global conflict; military and political outcomes unfolded in stages.
